Why this matters – Surveillance of P. aeruginosa
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a leading cause of healthcare‑associated infections, especially in immunocompromised patients, cystic fibrosis, and burn wounds. It exhibits both intrinsic and acquired resistance to many antibiotics, and its virulence arsenal (T3SS, exotoxin A, biofilms) makes infections difficult to treat.

This report provides a gene‑centric view – each resistance, virulence, plasmid, biocide‑metal, or mutation is shown with all genomes that carry it. This allows rapid identification of outbreak clones, co‑occurrence patterns, and potential co‑selection risks.

✨ Key Features of This Report

🧬 Gene‑Centric Tables

Each AMR, virulence, plasmid, bacmet, or mutation is displayed with the list of genomes that carry it – no more hunting through individual sample reports.

🔗 Dynamic Grouping by Typing

Group genomes by MLST, O‑type, or ST‑O combinations to instantly see which clones harbour specific genes or mutations.

📚 Comprehensive Database Integration

Combines AMRfinder, ABRicate (CARD, ResFinder, VFDB, PlasmidFinder, BacMet2, etc.) for maximum sensitivity and consensus.

🔍 Interactive Filters & Highlighting

Click buttons to focus on key gene families (carbapenemases, T3SS, biocide resistance, point mutations) and highlight specific isolates across tables.

🧩 ST‑O Combination Analysis

Identify epidemic clones (e.g., ST235‑O11) and their associated resistance/virulence profiles.

📊 FASTA QC Metrics

Assembly quality (N50, contig count) ensures reliable gene calls.

🧬 Mutation Tracking

Point mutations in gyrA, parC, rpoB, 23S rRNA, etc. – detect resistance even without acquired genes.

📤 Export & AI‑Ready

Export any table as CSV or download the complete JSON for upload to ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini for further analysis.

Population Structure Overview
Understanding the genetic background of your P. aeruginosa isolates is critical for outbreak tracking and risk assessment.
  • MLST (Sequence Type): Multilocus sequence typing (Pasteur scheme) defines STs. High‑risk clones (e.g., ST111, ST235, ST244, ST277) are often associated with carbapenem resistance and severe infections.
  • O‑Serotype: The lipopolysaccharide O‑antigen is a vaccine target. Prevalent types include O1, O2, O5, O6, O11. Serotype O11 is linked to epidemic clones.
  • N50: A key assembly quality metric (the shortest contig length such that half the genome is in contigs of that size or larger). Higher N50 = better assembly.
  • Virulence Count: Number of detected virulence genes from VFDB. Higher counts may indicate greater pathogenic potential.

FASTA QC – Powered by Biopython
Biopython by The Biopython Consortium Used for parsing FASTA files and computing quality metrics (GC%, N50, contig counts, etc.).
Biopython is an open‑source toolkit for computational biology, essential for robust and reproducible assembly QC.
FASTA Quality Control – Why It Matters
Assembly quality directly affects gene detection. Poor assemblies (low N50, high contig count) may miss genes or create false positives.
  • N50: Ideally >20 kb for accurate gene annotation.
  • Contig count: Fewer contigs (e.g., <200) indicate a more complete assembly.
  • GC%: P. aeruginosa typically 66–67%. Deviations may indicate contamination.

Important: Due to licensing restrictions on the PubMLST database, we cannot include alleles added after December 31, 2024. To use the latest alleles, you can update your local database by following the instructions from Seemann's MLST.
MLST (Pasteur scheme) – Tracking High‑Risk Clones
Multi‑locus sequence typing uses seven housekeeping genes (acsA, aroE, guaA, mutL, nuoD, ppsA, trpE). Globally disseminated high‑risk clones include:
  • ST111: Often carries VIM‑2 carbapenemase and ExoU; associated with ventilator‑associated pneumonia.
  • ST235: Major carbapenemase producer (KPC, NDM, VIM) with ExoU; pandemic clone.
  • ST244: Common in environmental and some clinical settings; often less virulent.
  • ST277: Associated with multidrug resistance and cystic fibrosis.

O‑Serotype (PAST) – A Vaccine Target
The O‑antigen is a major surface antigen and a component of the investigational vaccine for P. aeruginosa. Common serotypes in clinical isolates include O1, O2, O5, O6, and O11. Serotype O11 is often associated with epidemic multidrug‑resistant clones.

Knowing the serotype distribution can guide vaccine development and infection control.

PAST tool originally developed by the Technical University of Denmark (CGE). This implementation uses pasty by Dr. Robert A. Petit III, which makes the original PAst tool more user‑friendly and accessible for genomic surveillance. Original PAst‑1.0

Antimicrobial Resistance in P. aeruginosa – A Clinical Nightmare
P. aeruginosa exhibits both intrinsic resistance (e.g., AmpC β‑lactamase, efflux pumps MexAB‑OprM, low outer membrane permeability) and acquired resistance via mobile elements.

Critical resistance mechanisms to monitor:
  • Carbapenemases (KPC, NDM, VIM, IMP, OXA‑48‑like): Destroy last‑line antibiotics. Often plasmid‑borne and associated with high mortality.
  • ESBLs (GES, PER, VEB): Confer resistance to ceftazidime and aztreonam.
  • Colistin resistance (mcr genes, chromosomal mutations): Threatens last‑resort polymyxins.
  • 16S rRNA methyltransferases (armA, rmt): Cause high‑level aminoglycoside resistance.
  • Efflux pump upregulation (mexAB‑oprM, mexXY): Multidrug resistance.
Use filter buttons to focus on major classes. Genes marked with ⚠️ are critical for surveillance.

Virulence Factor Database (VFDB) via ABRicate
VFDB by The VFDB Consortium Integrated through ABRicate (Prof. Torsten Seemann).
Comprehensive resource for bacterial virulence factors, essential for understanding pathogenesis and identifying therapeutic targets.
Virulence Factors – What Makes P. aeruginosa So Dangerous?
P. aeruginosa possesses a large arsenal of virulence determinants that contribute to acute and chronic infections.
  • Type III Secretion System (T3SS) effectors: ExoU (phospholipase – highly cytotoxic, associated with poor outcomes), ExoS (ADP‑ribosyltransferase), ExoT, ExoY.
  • Exotoxin A (ToxA): Inhibits protein synthesis, similar to diphtheria toxin.
  • Elastases (LasB, LasA): Degrade host tissues and immune components.
  • Biofilm components (alginate, Psl, Pel): Essential for chronic infections (e.g., cystic fibrosis).
  • Siderophores (pyoverdine, pyochelin): Scavenge iron from host.
Genes marked with ⚠️ are critical for virulence and potential therapeutic targets.

PlasmidFinder – Replicon Typing via ABRicate
PlasmidFinder by CGE (Technical University of Denmark) Integrated through ABRicate (Prof. Torsten Seemann).
Identify plasmid replicon types to track horizontal gene transfer and outbreak dynamics.
Plasmid Replicons – Vehicles of Resistance
Plasmids are extrachromosomal elements that often carry AMR and virulence genes. Identifying replicon types helps track horizontal gene transfer.
  • IncP-2: Large plasmids often carrying carbapenemase genes (e.g., blaIMP, blaVIM).
  • IncQ: Broad‑host‑range plasmids, frequent carriers of aminoglycoside resistance.
  • IncU: Common in P. aeruginosa multidrug resistance plasmids.
  • Col plasmids: Carry colicin determinants, sometimes linked to virulence.
Knowing which plasmid families are circulating can reveal outbreak dynamics and guide infection control.

BacMet2 – Biocide & Metal Resistance Database via ABRicate
BacMet2 by The BacMet Consortium Integrated through ABRicate (Prof. Torsten Seemann).
Comprehensive resource for genes conferring resistance to biocides, heavy metals, and stress responses – critical for tracking co‑selection and infection control.
Bacmet2 – Biocide, Heavy Metal & Stress Resistance
These genes confer resistance to disinfectants (quaternary ammonium, chlorhexidine, formaldehyde), heavy metals (mercury, arsenic, copper, silver, chromium, cadmium, zinc, lead), and stress responses.

Why track them? Biocide resistance can compromise infection control measures (e.g., antiseptic wipes, surface disinfectants). Heavy metal resistance often co‑selects with AMR genes on the same mobile elements (co‑selection).
  • qac – Quaternary ammonium compound resistance (common in hospital disinfectants).
  • mer – Mercury resistance; often linked to transposons carrying AMR genes.
  • sil – Silver resistance; threatens use of silver‑based wound dressings.
  • soxR/cpxR – Stress regulators that activate efflux pumps and promote multidrug resistance.

Point Mutations – Gene‑Centric View + Grouping by Typing
Each unique mutation (gene + element name) is shown with all genomes that carry it. Mutations in key genes (e.g., gyrA, parC, rpoB, 23S rRNA) can confer resistance even without acquired resistance genes. Use grouping buttons to reorganise by typing and identify clones with specific mutational profiles.
Group genomes by:
Clinical relevance of key mutations in P. aeruginosa:
• 23S rRNA (linezolid) – Mutations (e.g., G2576T, T2500A) confer resistance to linezolid, a last‑line antibiotic for MRSA/VRE.
• gyrA/parC (quinolones) – Mutations in the quinolone resistance‑determining region (QRDR) reduce susceptibility to fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin).
• rpoB (rifampin) – Mutations cause high‑level rifampin resistance, often used in combination therapy.
• mprF (daptomycin) – Mutations can lead to daptomycin non‑susceptibility.
• rplC/rplD (linezolid) – Ribosomal protein mutations also confer linezolid resistance.

Cross‑Genome Patterns – Tracking Clones and Co‑occurrence
This section shows:
  • ST‑O combination table: Which Sequence Types are associated with which O‑serotypes? Certain ST‑O pairs (e.g., ST235‑O11) define epidemic clones.
  • Gene co‑occurrence: Which pairs of genes (AMR, virulence, plasmid, bacmet) are frequently found together in the same genome. High co‑occurrence may indicate co‑selection or physical linkage (e.g., on the same plasmid).
Use these tables to identify outbreak clones and potential co‑selection risks.

📚 How to Cite GENIUS P. aeruginosa Ultimate Reporter and Its Dependencies

If you use this tool in your research, please cite the main tool and the relevant third‑party tools and databases.

PseudoScope – Beckley B, Amarh V. PseudoScope: a species‑specific bioinformatics suite for rapid and accessible Pseudomonas aeruginosa genomic analysis. Github 2026 https://github.com/brown-beckley/pseudoscope
MLST (Pasteur scheme) – Seemann T. MLST: Scan contig files against PubMLST typing schemes. GitHub. https://github.com/tseemann/mlst
PAST (P. aeruginosa serotyping) – Jolley KA, Bray JE, Maiden MCJ. Open‑access bacterial population genomics: BIGSdb software, the PubMLST.org website and their applications. Wellcome Open Res. 2018;3:124. 10.12688/wellcomeopenres.14826.1
AMRFinderPlus – Feldgarden M, et al. AMRFinderPlus and the Reference Gene Catalog facilitate examination of the genomic links among antimicrobial resistance, stress response, and virulence. Sci Rep. 2021;11(1):12728. 10.1038/s41598-021-91456-0
ABRicate – Seemann T. ABRicate: mass screening of contigs for antibiotic resistance genes. GitHub. https://github.com/tseemann/abricate
CARD – McArthur AG, et al. The comprehensive antibiotic resistance database. Antimicrob Agents Chemother. 2013;57(7):3348-57. 10.1128/AAC.00419-13
ResFinder – Florensa AF, et al. ResFinder – an open online resource for identification of antimicrobial resistance genes in next‑generation sequencing data and prediction of phenotypes from genotypes. Microb Genom. 2022;8(1):000748. 10.1099/mgen.0.000748
VFDB – Chen L, et al. VFDB 2012 update: toward the genetic diversity and molecular evolution of bacterial virulence factors. Nucleic Acids Res. 2012;40(Database issue):D641-5. 10.1093/nar/gkr989
PlasmidFinder – Carattoli A, et al. In silico detection and typing of plasmids using PlasmidFinder and plasmid multilocus sequence typing. Antimicrob Agents Chemother. 2014;58(7):3895-903. 10.1128/AAC.02412-14
BacMet – Pal C, et al. BacMet: antibacterial biocide and metal resistance genes database. Nucleic Acids Res. 2014;42(Database issue):D737-43. 10.1093/nar/gkt1252
MEGARes – Doster E, et al. MEGARes 2.0: a database for classification of antimicrobial drug, biocide and metal resistance determinants in metagenomic sequence data. Nucleic Acids Res. 2020;48(D1):D561-D569. 10.1093/nar/gkz1010
Biopython – Cock PJ, et al. Biopython: freely available Python tools for computational molecular biology and bioinformatics. Bioinformatics. 2009;25(11):1422-3. 10.1093/bioinformatics/btp163
Suggested acknowledgement:
"Genomic analysis was performed using PseudoScope [Beckley & Amarh, 2026] which integrates MLST [Seemann, 2018] using the PubMLST database [Jolley et al., 2018], ABRicate [Seemann, 2018], AMRFinderPlus [Feldgarden et al., 2021], and PAST serotyping for comprehensive P. aeruginosa characterization. Antimicrobial resistance genes were identified using the CARD [McArthur et al., 2013] and ResFinder [Florensa et al., 2022] databases. For biocide and heavy metal resistance genes, BacMet [Pal et al., 2014] was used. Virulence and plasmid screening were performed with ABRicate using the VFDB [Chen et al., 2012] and PlasmidFinder [Carattoli et al., 2014] databases."

📘 Welcome to GENIUS P. aeruginosa Ultimate Report – Your Guide

This guide explains how to get the most out of each tab, why multiple databases are used, and some practical tips (with a touch of humour).

How to Use the Report

  • Summary – Overview of your dataset and key statistics.
  • Sample Overview – List of all samples with ST, O‑type, and virulence counts.
  • FASTA QC – Assembly quality metrics. Good assemblies = reliable gene calls.
  • MLST – ST distribution and sample lists. High‑risk clones are highlighted in the notes.
  • O‑Serotype – Serotype distribution with genome tags. Use highlight to track specific isolates.
  • AMR Genes – Gene‑centric table of resistance genes. Use the grouping buttons (ST, O‑type, ST‑O) to see which clones carry which genes. Filter buttons for major resistance families.
  • Virulence – Same grouping and filtering for virulence factors. Identify hypervirulent clones.
  • Plasmid Replicons – Plasmid types that can carry resistance genes.
  • Bacmet2 – Biocide and heavy metal resistance genes – important for hospital hygiene.
  • Mutations – Point mutations that can confer resistance. Group and filter to see which clones have specific mutational profiles.
  • Patterns – ST‑O combinations and gene co‑occurrence. Find outbreak clones and co‑selection links.
  • Citation – All required citations, copy‑able with one click, with distinct coloured cards.
  • Call to Action – Learn about the global AMR burden and how you can contribute.
  • Export – Download tables as CSV and full JSON for AI or downstream analysis.

Why Multiple Databases?

Some users ask: "Why use AMRfinder and ABRicate with CARD, ResFinder, and NCBI?"

Because no single database is perfect. Each has strengths and biases. For example:

  • AMRfinder – Curated by NCBI, excellent for clinically relevant genes, but may miss some environmental or novel variants.
  • CARD – Comprehensive with detailed resistance mechanisms, but often lag behind newly discovered genes.
  • ResFinder – Frequently updated and widely used in clinical labs, but focuses on acquired resistance.
  • NCBI – Large but sometimes includes non‑specific hits.

By combining them, we maximise sensitivity and provide a consensus view. If a gene appears in multiple databases, it's a strong signal. If only one, it's worth double‑checking. Humour: Think of it like asking three friends what happened at the party – you get the full story, not just one biased version. 😄

Also, some databases perform better for certain species or gene families. For P. aeruginosa, CARD and ResFinder are generally excellent, but AMRfinder catches many carbapenemase variants. We give you all the data, you decide what to trust.

Pro Tips

  • Grouping – In AMR, Virulence, Plasmid, Bacmet, and Mutation tabs, click "Group by ST" or "Group by O‑type" to instantly see which clones harbour specific genes or mutations. This is incredibly powerful for outbreak tracking.
  • Highlighting – Use the "Highlight sample" search boxes to find a particular isolate across all tables – it will turn yellow!
  • Export – You can export any table as CSV. The JSON file is ideal for AI tools – upload it to ChatGPT/Claude and ask questions about your data.
  • Print – Each section has a print button to save as PDF for reports.

The Global Burden of AMR and Our Call to Action

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) kills an estimated 1.27 million people directly each year. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a WHO critical‑priority pathogen, especially when carbapenem‑resistant. Genomic surveillance is our best tool to track resistant clones, understand transmission, and guide infection control.

We developed GENIUS P. aeruginosa Ultimate Reporter as part of the ESCAPE AMR project – an open‑source initiative targeting all ESKAPE pathogens. Our goal is to empower researchers, especially in low‑resource settings, with user‑friendly genomic analysis tools.

ESCAPE AMR – Our Vision

We believe the name “ESCAPE” is also a call to action:

  • Everyone must join forces – researchers, clinicians, policymakers.
  • Smart surveillance is our first line of defence – sequence, don’t guess.
  • Knowledge must be shared openly – no paywalls, no silos.
  • Africa bears a heavy AMR burden, but African solutions are emerging.
  • Prevention is cheaper than cure – let’s stop resistant infections before they spread.
  • Every day we delay, more lives are at stake – act now.
